<div sID="gen26847" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="4" osisID="John.4" sID="John.4"/> <div eID="gen26847" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26848" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen26849" type="x-p"/> It was, more than any thing else, the glory of the land of Israel, that it was Emmanuel's land (<reference osisRef="Isa.8.8">Isa. viii. 8</reference>), not only the place of his birth, but the scene of his preaching and miracles. This land in our Saviour's time was divided into three parts: Judea in the south, Galilee in the north, and Samaria lying between them. Now, in this chapter, we have Christ in each of these three parts of that land. I. Departing out of Judea, <reference osisRef="John.4.1-John.4.3">ver. 1-3</reference>. II. Passing through Samaria, which, though a visit in transitu, here takes up most room. 1. His coming into Samaria, <reference osisRef="John.4.4-John.4.6">ver. 4-6</reference>. 2. His discourse with the Samaritan woman at a well, <reference osisRef="John.4.7-John.4.26">ver. 7-26</reference>. 3. The notice which the woman gave of him to the city, <reference osisRef="John.4.27-John.4.30">ver. 27-30</reference>. 4. Christ's talk with his disciples in the meantime, <reference osisRef="John.4.31-John.4.38">ver. 31-38</reference>. 5. The good effect of this among the Samaritans, <reference osisRef="John.4.39-John.4.42">ver. 39-42</reference>. III. We find him residing for some time in Galilee (<reference osisRef="John.4.43-John.4.46">ver. 43-46</reference>), and his curing a nobleman's son there, that was at death's door, <reference osisRef="John.4.46-John.4.54">ver. 46-54</reference>.

entries.content_osis: <div eID="gen26849" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen26848" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Christ's Journey into Galilee.</title> <div sID="gen26850" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> When therefore the Lord knew how the Pharisees had heard that Jesus made and baptized more disciples than John, 2 (Though Jesus himself baptized not, but his disciples,) 3 He left Judæa, and departed again into Galilee. <div eID="gen26850" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26851" type="x-p"/> We read of Christ's coming into Judea (<reference osisRef="John.3.22">ch. iii. 22</reference>), after he had kept the feast at Jerusalem; and now he left Judea four months before harvest, as is said here (<reference osisRef="John.4.35">v. 35</reference>); so that it is computed that he staid in Judea about six months, to build upon the foundation John had laid there. We have no particular account of his sermons and miracles there, only in general, <reference osisRef="John.4.1">v. 1</reference>. <div eID="gen26851" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26852" type="x-p"/> I. That he <hi type="italic">made disciples;</hi> he prevailed with many to embrace his doctrine, and to follow him as a teacher come from God. His ministry was successful, notwithstanding the opposition it met with (<reference osisRef="Ps.110.2-Ps.110.3">Ps. cx. 2, 3</reference>); <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">mathetas poiei</hi></hi>—it signifies the same with <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">matheteuo</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">to disciples.</hi> Compare <reference osisRef="Gen.12.5">Gen. xii. 5</reference>. <hi type="italic">The souls which they had gotten,</hi> which they had <hi type="italic">made</hi> (so the word is), which they had <hi type="italic">made proselytes.</hi> Note, It is Christ's prerogative to <hi type="italic">make disciples,</hi> first to bring them to his foot, and then to form and fashion them to his will. <hi type="italic">Fit, non nascitur, Christianus—The Christian is made such, not born such.</hi> Tertullian. <div eID="gen26852" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26853" type="x-p"/> II. That he <hi type="italic">baptized</hi> those whom he <hi type="italic">made disciples,</hi> admitted them by <hi type="italic">washing them with water;</hi> not himself, but by the ministry of his disciples, <reference osisRef="John.4.2">v. 2</reference>. 1. Because he would put a difference between his baptism and that of John, who baptized all himself; for he baptized as a servant, Christ as a master. 2. He would apply himself more to preaching work, which was the more excellent, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.17">1 Cor. i. 17</reference>. 3. He would put honour upon his disciples, by empowering and employing them to do it; and so train them up to further services. 4. If he had baptized some himself, they would have been apt to value themselves upon that, and despise others, which he would prevent, as Paul, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.13-1Cor.1.14">1 Cor. i. 13, 14</reference>. 5. He would reserve himself for the honour of baptizing with the Holy Ghost, <reference osisRef="Acts.1.5">Acts i. 5</reference>. 6. He would teach us that the efficacy of the sacraments depends not on any virtue in the hand that administers them, as also that what is done by his ministers, according to his direction, he owns as done by himself. <div eID="gen26853" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26854" type="x-p"/> III. That he made and baptized <hi type="italic">more disciples than John;</hi> not only more than John did at this time, but more than he had done at any time. Christ's converse was more winning than John's. His miracles were convincing, and the cures he wrought <hi type="italic">gratis</hi> very inviting. <div eID="gen26854" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26855" type="x-p"/> IV. That the Pharisees were informed of this; they heard what multitudes he baptized, for they had, from his first appearing, a jealous eye upon him, and wanted not spies to give them notice concerning him. Observe, 1. When the Pharisees thought they had got rid of John (for he was by this time imprisoned), and were pleasing themselves with that, Jesus appears, who was a greater vexation to them than ever John had been. The witnesses will rise again. 2. That which grieved them was that Christ made so many disciples. The success of the gospel exasperates its enemies, and it is a good sign that it is getting ground when the powers of darkness are enraged against it. <div eID="gen26855" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26856" type="x-p"/> V. That our Lord Jesus knew very well what informations were given in against him to the Pharisees. It is probable the informers were willing to have their names concealed, and the Pharisees loth to have their designs known; but none can dig so keep as to <hi type="italic">hide their counsels from the Lord</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.29.15">Isa. xxix. 15</reference>), and Christ is here called <hi type="italic">the Lord.</hi> He knew what was told the Pharisees, and how much, it is likely, it exceeded the truth; for it is not likely that Jesus had yet baptized <hi type="italic">more than John;</hi> but so the thing was represented, to make him appear the more formidable; see <reference osisRef="2Kgs.6.12">2 Kings vi. 12</reference>. <div eID="gen26856" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26857" type="x-p"/> VI. That hereupon our Lord Jesus <hi type="italic">left Judea</hi> and <hi type="italic">departed again</hi> to go to Galilee. <div eID="gen26857" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26858" type="x-p"/> 1. He <hi type="italic">left Judea,</hi> because he was likely to be persecuted there even to the death; such was the rage of the Pharisees against him, and such their impious policy to devour the man-child in his infancy. To escape their designs, Christ quitted the country, and went where what he did would be less provoking than just under their eye. For, (1.) His hour was not yet come (<reference osisRef="John.7.30">ch. vii. 30</reference>), the time fixed in the counsels of God, and the Old-Testament prophecies, for Messiah's being cut off. He had not finished his testimony, and therefore would not surrender or expose himself. (2.) The disciples he had gathered in Judea were not able to bear hardships, and therefore he would not expose them. (3.) Hereby he gave an example to his own rule: <hi type="italic">When they persecute you in one city, flee to another.</hi> We are not called to suffer, while we may avoid it without sin; and therefore, though we may not, for our own preservation, change our religion, yet we may change our place. Christ secured himself, not by a miracle, but in a way <hi type="italic">common to men,</hi> for the direction and encouragement of his suffering people. <div eID="gen26858" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26859" type="x-p"/> 2. He departed into Galilee, because he had work to do there, and many friends and fewer enemies. He went to Galilee now, (1.) Because John's ministry had now <hi type="italic">made way</hi> for him there; for Galilee, which was under Herod's jurisdiction, was the last scene of John's baptism. (2.) Because John's imprisonment had now <hi type="italic">made room</hi> for him there. That light being now put under a bushel, the minds of people would not be divided between him and Christ. Thus both the liberties and restraints of good ministers are for the furtherance of the gospel, <reference osisRef="Phil.1.12">Phil. i. 12</reference>. But to what purpose does he go into Galilee for safety? Herod, the persecutor of John, will never be the protector of Jesus. Chemnitius here notes, <hi type="italic">Pii in h&#225;c vit&#180; quos fugiant habent; ad quos vero fugiant ut in tuto sint non habent, nisi ad te, Deus, qui solus regugium nostrum es</hi>—<hi type="italic">The pious have those, in this life, to whom they can fly; but they have none to fly to, who can afford them refuge, except thee, O God.</hi>
entries.content_plain: Christ's Journey into Galilee. 1 When therefore the Lord knew how the Pharisees had heard that Jesus made and baptized more disciples than John, 2 (Though Jesus himself baptized not, but his disciples,) 3 He left Judæa, and departed again into Galilee. We read of Christ's coming into Judea ( ch. iii. 22 ), after he had kept the feast at Jerusalem; and now he left Judea four months before harvest, as is said here ( v. 35 ); so that it is computed that he staid in Judea about six months, to build upon the foundation John had laid there. We have no particular account of his sermons and miracles there, only in general, v. 1 . I. That he made disciples; he prevailed with many to embrace his doctrine, and to follow him as a teacher come from God. His ministry was successful, notwithstanding the opposition it met with ( Ps. cx. 2, 3 ); mathetas poiei —it signifies the same with matheteuo — to disciples. Compare Gen. xii. 5 . The souls which they had gotten, which they had made (so the word is), which they had made proselytes. Note, It is Christ's prerogative to make disciples, first to bring them to his foot, and then to form and fashion them to his will. Fit, non nascitur, Christianus—The Christian is made such, not born such. Tertullian. II. That he baptized those whom he made disciples, admitted them by washing them with water; not himself, but by the ministry of his disciples, v. 2 . 1. Because he would put a difference between his baptism and that of John, who baptized all himself; for he baptized as a servant, Christ as a master. 2. He would apply himself more to preaching work, which was the more excellent, 1 Cor. i. 17 . 3. He would put honour upon his disciples, by empowering and employing them to do it; and so train them up to further services. 4. If he had baptized some himself, they would have been apt to value themselves upon that, and despise others, which he would prevent, as Paul, 1 Cor. i. 13, 14 . 5. He would reserve himself for the honour of baptizing with the Holy Ghost, Acts i. 5 . 6. He would teach us that the efficacy of the sacraments depends not on any virtue in the hand that administers them, as also that what is done by his ministers, according to his direction, he owns as done by himself. III. That he made and baptized more disciples than John; not only more than John did at this time, but more than he had done at any time. Christ's converse was more winning than John's. His miracles were convincing, and the cures he wrought gratis very inviting. IV. That the Pharisees were informed of this; they heard what multitudes he baptized, for they had, from his first appearing, a jealous eye upon him, and wanted not spies to give them notice concerning him. Observe, 1. When the Pharisees thought they had got rid of John (for he was by this time imprisoned), and were pleasing themselves with that, Jesus appears, who was a greater vexation to them than ever John had been. The witnesses will rise again. 2. That which grieved them was that Christ made so many disciples. The success of the gospel exasperates its enemies, and it is a good sign that it is getting ground when the powers of darkness are enraged against it. V. That our Lord Jesus knew very well what informations were given in against him to the Pharisees. It is probable the informers were willing to have their names concealed, and the Pharisees loth to have their designs known; but none can dig so keep as to hide their counsels from the Lord ( Isa. xxix. 15 ), and Christ is here called the Lord. He knew what was told the Pharisees, and how much, it is likely, it exceeded the truth; for it is not likely that Jesus had yet baptized more than John; but so the thing was represented, to make him appear the more formidable; see 2 Kings vi. 12 . VI. That hereupon our Lord Jesus left Judea and departed again to go to Galilee. 1. He left Judea, because he was likely to be persecuted there even to the death; such was the rage of the Pharisees against him, and such their impious policy to devour the man-child in his infancy. To escape their designs, Christ quitted the country, and went where what he did would be less provoking than just under their eye. For, (1.) His hour was not yet come ( ch. vii. 30 ), the time fixed in the counsels of God, and the Old-Testament prophecies, for Messiah's being cut off. He had not finished his testimony, and therefore would not surrender or expose himself. (2.) The disciples he had gathered in Judea were not able to bear hardships, and therefore he would not expose them. (3.) Hereby he gave an example to his own rule: When they persecute you in one city, flee to another. We are not called to suffer, while we may avoid it without sin; and therefore, though we may not, for our own preservation, change our religion, yet we may change our place. Christ secured himself, not by a miracle, but in a way common to men, for the direction and encouragement of his suffering people. 2. He departed into Galilee, because he had work to do there, and many friends and fewer enemies. He went to Galilee now, (1.) Because John's ministry had now made way for him there; for Galilee, which was under Herod's jurisdiction, was the last scene of John's baptism. (2.) Because John's imprisonment had now made room for him there. That light being now put under a bushel, the minds of people would not be divided between him and Christ. Thus both the liberties and restraints of good ministers are for the furtherance of the gospel, Phil. i. 12 . But to what purpose does he go into Galilee for safety? Herod, the persecutor of John, will never be the protector of Jesus. Thus both the liberties and restraints of good ministers are for the furtherance of the gospel, <reference osisRef="Phil.1.12">Phil. i. 12</reference>. But to what purpose does he go into Galilee for safety? Herod, the persecutor of John, will never be the protector of Jesus. Chemnitius here notes, <hi type="italic">Pii in h&#225;c vit&#180; quos fugiant habent; ad quos vero fugiant ut in tuto sint non habent, nisi ad te, Deus, qui solus regugium nostrum es</hi>—<hi type="italic">The pious have those, in this life, to whom they can fly; but they have none to fly to, who can afford them refuge, except thee, O God.</hi>

entries.content_osis: <div eID="gen26859" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Christ at the Well of Samaria.</title> <div sID="gen26860" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">4</hi> And he must needs go through Samaria. <hi type="super">5</hi> Then cometh he to a city of Samaria, which is called Sychar, near to the parcel of ground that Jacob gave to his son Joseph. <hi type="super">6</hi> Now Jacob's well was there. Jesus therefore, being wearied with <hi type="italic">his</hi> journey, sat thus on the well: <hi type="italic">and</hi> it was about the sixth hour. <hi type="super">7</hi> There cometh a woman of Samaria to draw water: Jesus saith unto her, Give me to drink. <hi type="super">8</hi> (For his disciples were gone away unto the city to buy meat.) <hi type="super">9</hi> Then saith the woman of Samaria unto him, How is it that thou, being a Jew, askest drink of me, which am a woman of Samaria? for the Jews have no dealings with the Samaritans. <hi type="super">10</hi> Jesus answered and said unto her, If thou knewest the gift of God, and who it is that saith to thee, Give me to drink; thou wouldest have asked of him, and he would have given thee living water. <hi type="super">11</hi> The woman saith unto him, Sir, thou hast nothing to draw with, and the well is deep: from whence then hast thou that living water? <hi type="super">12</hi> Art thou greater than our father Jacob, which gave us the well, and drank thereof himself, and his children, and his cattle? <hi type="super">13</hi> Jesus answered and said unto her, Whosoever drinketh of this water shall thirst again: <hi type="super">14</hi> But whosoever drinketh of the water that I shall give him shall never thirst; but the water that I shall give him shall be in him a well of water springing up into everlasting life. <hi type="super">15</hi> The woman saith unto him, Sir, give me this water, that I thirst not, neither come hither to draw. <hi type="super">16</hi> Jesus saith unto her, Go, call thy husband, and come hither. 17 The woman answered and said, I have no husband. Jesus said unto her, Thou hast well said, I have no husband: <hi type="super">18</hi> For thou hast had five husbands; and he whom thou now hast is not thy husband: in that saidst thou truly. <hi type="super">19</hi> The woman saith unto him, Sir, I perceive that thou art a prophet. <hi type="super">20</hi> Our fathers worshipped in this mountain; and ye say, that in Jerusalem is the place where men ought to worship. <hi type="super">21</hi> Jesus saith unto her, Woman, believe me, the hour cometh, when ye shall neither in this mountain, nor yet at Jerusalem, worship the Father. <hi type="super">22</hi> Ye worship ye know not what: we know what we worship: for salvation is of the Jews. <hi type="super">23</hi> But the hour cometh, and now is, when the true worshippers shall worship the Father in spirit and in truth: for the Father seeketh such to worship him. <hi type="super">24</hi> God <hi type="italic">is</hi> a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship <hi type="italic">him</hi> in spirit and in truth. <hi type="super">25</hi> The woman saith unto him, I know that Messias cometh, which is called Christ: when he is come, he will tell us all things. <hi type="super">26</hi> Jesus saith unto her, I that speak unto thee am <hi type="italic">he.</hi> <div eID="gen26860" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26861" type="x-p"/> We have here an account of the good Christ did in Samaria, when he <hi type="italic">passed through</hi> that country in his way to Galilee. The Samaritans, both in <hi type="italic">blood</hi> and <hi type="italic">religion,</hi> were <hi type="italic">mongrel Jews,</hi> the posterity of those colonies which the king of Assyria planted there after the captivity of the ten tribes, with whom the poor of the land that were left behind, and many other Jews afterwards, incorporated themselves. They worshipped the God of Israel only, to whom they erected a temple on mount Gerizim, in competition with that at Jerusalem. There was great enmity between them and the Jews; the Samaritans would not admit Christ, when they saw he was going to Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="Luke.9.53">Luke ix. 53</reference>); the Jews thought they could not give him a worse name than to say, <hi type="italic">He is a Samaritan.</hi> When the Jews were in prosperity, the Samaritans claimed kindred to them (<reference osisRef="Ezra.4.2">Ezra iv. 2</reference>), but, when the Jews were in distress, they were Medes and Persians; see Joseph. <hi type="italic">Antiq.</hi> 11. 340-341; 12. 257. Now observe, <div eID="gen26861" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26862" type="x-p"/> I. Christ's coming into Samaria. He charged his disciples not to <hi type="italic">enter into any city of the Samaritans</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.10.5">Matt. x. 5</reference>), that is, not to preach the gospel, or work miracles; nor did he here preach publicly, or work any miracle, his eye being to <hi type="italic">the lost sheep of the house of Israel.</hi> What kindness he here did them was <hi type="italic">accidental;</hi> it was only a <hi type="italic">crumb</hi> of the children's bread that casually <hi type="italic">fell from the master's table.</hi> <div eID="gen26862" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26863" type="x-p"/> 1. His <hi type="italic">road</hi> from Judea to Galilee lay through the <hi type="italic">country</hi> of Samaria (<reference osisRef="John.4.4">v. 4</reference>): <hi type="italic">He must needs go through Samaria.</hi> There was no other way, unless he would have fetched a compass on the other side <hi type="italic">Jordan,</hi> a great way about. The wicked and profane are at present so intermixed with God's Israel that, unless we will go <hi type="italic">out of the world,</hi> we cannot avoid <hi type="italic">going through</hi> the company of such, <reference osisRef="1Cor.5.10">1 Cor. v. 10</reference>. We have therefore need of the armour or righteousness on the right hand and on the left, that we may neither give <hi type="italic">provocation</hi> to them nor contract <hi type="italic">pollution</hi> by them. We should not go into places of temptation but when we <hi type="italic">needs must;</hi> and then we should not reside in them, but <hi type="italic">hasten through</hi> them. Some think that Christ <hi type="italic">must needs</hi> go through Samaria because of the good work he had to do there; a poor woman to be converted, a lost sheep to be sought and saved. This was work his heart was upon, the <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> he <hi type="italic">must needs</hi> go this way. It was happy for Samaria that it lay <hi type="italic">in Christ's way,</hi> which gave him an opportunity of calling on them. <hi type="italic">When I passed by thee, I said unto thee, Live,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.16.6">Ezek. xvi. 6</reference>. <div eID="gen26863" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26864" type="x-p"/> 2. His baiting place happened to be at a <hi type="italic">city of Samaria.</hi> Now observe, <div eID="gen26864" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26865" type="x-p"/> (1.) The place described. It was called <hi type="italic">Sychar;</hi> probably the same with <hi type="italic">Sichem,</hi> or <hi type="italic">Shechem,</hi> a place which we read much of in the Old Testament. Thus are the names of places commonly corrupted by tract of time. Shechem yielded the first proselyte that ever came into the church of Israel (<reference osisRef="Gen.34.24">Gen. xxxiv. 24</reference>), and now it is the first place where the gospel is preached out of the commonwealth of Israel; so Dr. Lightfoot observes; as also that the <hi type="italic">valley of Achor,</hi> which was given for a <hi type="italic">door of hope,</hi> hope to the poor Gentiles, ran along by this city, <reference osisRef="Hos.2.15">Hos. ii. 15</reference>. Abimelech was made king here; it was Jeroboam's royal seat; but the evangelist, when he would give us the antiquities of the place, takes notice of Jacob's interest there, which was more its honour than its crowned heads. [1.] Here lay Jacob's ground, the <hi type="italic">parcel of ground which Jacob</hi> gave to his son Joseph, whose bones were buried in it, <reference osisRef="Gen.48.22">Gen. xlviii. 22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.24.32">Josh. xxiv. 32</reference>. Probably this is mentioned to intimate that Christ, when he reposed himself hard by here, took occasion from the ground which Jacob gave Joseph to meditate on the good report which the elders by faith obtained. Jerome chose to live in the land of Canaan, that the sight of the places might affect him the more with scripture stories. [2.] Here was Jacob's well which he digged, or at least used, for himself and his family. We find no mention of this well in the Old Testament; but the tradition was that it was Jacob's well. <div eID="gen26865" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26866" type="x-p"/> (2.) The posture of our Lord Jesus at this place: <hi type="italic">Being wearied with his journey, he sat thus on the well.</hi> We have here our Lord Jesus, <div eID="gen26866" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26867" type="x-p"/> [1.] Labouring under the common fatigue of travellers. He was <hi type="italic">wearied with his journey.</hi> Though it was yet but the sixth hour, and he had performed but half his day's journey, yet he was weary; or, <hi type="italic">because</hi> it was the sixth hour, the time of the heat of the day, therefore he was weary. Here we see, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> That he was a <hi type="italic">true man,</hi> and subject to the common infirmities of the human nature. Toil came in with sin (<reference osisRef="Gen.3.19">Gen. iii. 19</reference>), and therefore Christ, having made himself a curse for us, submitted to it. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> That he was a <hi type="italic">poor man,</hi> else he might have travelled on horseback or in a chariot. To this instance of meanness and mortification he humbled himself for us, that he went all his journeys on foot. When <hi type="italic">servants</hi> were on <hi type="italic">horses, princes walked as servants on the earth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eccl.10.7">Eccl. x. 7</reference>. When we are carried easily, let us think on the weariness of our Master. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> It should seem that he was but a <hi type="italic">tender man,</hi> and not of a robust constitution; it should seem, his disciples were not tired, for they went into the town without any difficulty, when their Master sat down, and could not go a step further. Bodies of the finest mould are most sensible of fatigue, and can worst bear it. <div eID="gen26867" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26868" type="x-p"/> [2.] We have him here betaking himself to the common relief of travellers; <hi type="italic">Being wearied, he sat thus on the well. First,</hi> He sat <hi type="italic">on the well,</hi> an <hi type="italic">uneasy place,</hi> cold and hard; he had no couch, no easy chair to repose himself in, but took to that which was <hi type="italic">next hand,</hi> to teach us not to be nice and curious in the conveniences of this life, but content with <hi type="italic">mean things. Secondly,</hi> He sat <hi type="italic">thus,</hi> in an <hi type="italic">uneasy posture;</hi> sat <hi type="italic">carelessly—incuriose et neglectim;</hi> or he sat <hi type="italic">so</hi> as people that are wearied with travelling are accustomed to sit. <div eID="gen26868" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26869" type="x-p"/> II. His discourse with a Samaritan woman, which is here recorded at large, while Christ's dispute with the doctors, and his discourse with Moses and Elias on the mount, are buried in silence. This discourse is reducible to four heads:— <div eID="gen26869" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26870" type="x-p"/> 1. They discourse <hi type="italic">concerning the water,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.4.7-John.4.15">v. 7-15</reference>. <div eID="gen26870" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26871" type="x-p"/> (1.) Notice is taken of the <hi type="italic">circumstances</hi> that gave occasion to this discourse. <div eID="gen26871" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26872" type="x-p"/> [1.] There comes a <hi type="italic">woman</hi> of Samaria to <hi type="italic">draw water.</hi> This intimates her poverty, she had no servant to be a <hi type="italic">drawer of water;</hi> and her industry, she would do it herself. See here, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> How God owns and approves of honest humble diligence in our places. Christ was made known to the shepherds when they were keeping their flock. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> How the divine Providence brings about glorious purposes by events which seem to us fortuitous and accidental. This woman's meeting with Christ at the well may remind us of the stories of Rebekah, Rachel, and Jethro's daughter, who all met with husbands, good husbands, no worse than Isaac, Jacob, and Moses, when they came to the wells for water. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> How the preventing grace of God sometimes brings people unexpectedly under the means of conversion and salvation. He is found of them that sought him not. <div eID="gen26872" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26873" type="x-p"/> [2.] His disciples were <hi type="italic">gone away into the city to buy meat.</hi> Hence learn a lesson, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Of justice and honesty. The meat Christ ate, he bought and paid for, as Paul, <reference osisRef="2Thess.3.8">2 Thess. iii. 8</reference>. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Of daily dependence upon Providence: <hi type="italic">Take no thought for the morrow.</hi> Christ did not go into the city to eat, but sent his disciples to fetch his meat thither; not because he scrupled eating in a Samaritan city, but, 1. Because he had a good work to do at that well, which might be done while they were catering. It is wisdom to fill up our vacant minutes with that which is good, that the <hi type="italic">fragments</hi> of time may <hi type="italic">not be lost.</hi> Peter, while his dinner was getting ready, fell into a trance, <reference osisRef="Acts.10.10">Acts x. 10</reference>. 2. Because it was more private and retired, more cheap and homely, to have his dinner brought him hither, than to go into the town for it. Perhaps his purse was low, and he would teach us <hi type="italic">good husbandry,</hi> to <hi type="italic">spend</hi> according to what we <hi type="italic">have</hi> and not go beyond it. At least, he would teach us not to affect great things. Christ could eat his dinner as well upon a <hi type="italic">draw well</hi> as in the best inn in the town. Let us <hi type="italic">comport</hi> with our circumstances. Now this gave Christ an opportunity of discoursing with this woman about spiritual concerns, and he improved it; he often preached to multitudes that crowded after him for instruction, yet here he condescends to teach a single person, a woman, a poor woman, a stranger, a Samaritan, to teach his ministers to do likewise, as those that know what a glorious achievement it is to help to save, though but <hi type="italic">one soul,</hi> from death. <div eID="gen26873" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26874" type="x-p"/> (2.) Let us observe the <hi type="italic">particulars</hi> of this discourse. <div eID="gen26874" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26875" type="x-p"/> [1.] Jesus begins with a modest request for a draught of water: <hi type="italic">Give me to drink.</hi> He that <hi type="italic">for our sakes became poor</hi> here becomes a beggar, that those who are in want, and cannot dig, may not be ashamed to beg. Christ asked for it, not only because he needed it, and needed her help to come at it, but because he would draw on further discourse with her, and teach us to be willing to be beholden to the meanest when there is occasion. Christ is still begging in his poor members, and a <hi type="italic">cup of cold water,</hi> like this here, given to them in his name, shall not lose its reward. <div eID="gen26875" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26876" type="x-p"/> [2.] The woman, though she does not deny his request, yet quarrels with him because he did not carry on the humour of his own nation (<reference osisRef="John.4.9">v. 9</reference>): <hi type="italic">How is it?</hi> Observe, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> What a mortal feud there was between the Jews and the Samaritans: <hi type="italic">The Jews have no dealings with the Samaritans.</hi> The Samaritans were the <hi type="italic">adversaries of Judah</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezra.4.1">Ezra iv. 1</reference>), were upon all occasions mischievous to them. The Jews were extremely malicious against the Samaritans, "looked upon them as having no part in the resurrection, excommunicated and cursed them by the sacred name of God, by the glorious writing of the tables, and by the curse of the upper and lower house of judgment, with this law, That no Israelite eat of any thing that is a Samaritan's, for it is as if he should eat swine's flesh." So Dr. Lightfoot, out of <hi type="italic">Rabbi Tanchum.</hi> Note, Quarrels about religion are usually the most implacable of all quarrels. Men were made to <hi type="italic">have dealing</hi> one with another; but if men, because one worships at one temple and another at another, will deny the offices of humanity, and charity, and common civility, will be morose and unnatural, scornful and censorious, and this under colour of zeal for religion, they plainly show that however their religion may be <hi type="italic">true</hi> they are not <hi type="italic">truly religious;</hi> but, pretending to stickle for religion, subvert the design of it. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> How ready the woman was to upbraid Christ with the haughtiness and ill nature of the Jewish nation: <hi type="italic">How is it that thou, being a Jew, askest drink of me?</hi> By his dress or dialect, or both, she knew him to be a Jew, and <hi type="italic">thinks it strange</hi> that he runs not to the same excess of riot against the Samaritans with other Jews. Note, Moderate men of all sides are, like Joshua and his fellows (<reference osisRef="Zech.3.8">Zech. iii. 8</reference>), <hi type="italic">men wondered at.</hi> Two things this woman wonders at, 1. That he should <hi type="italic">ask</hi> this kindness; for it was the pride of the Jews that they would endure any hardship rather than be beholden to a Samaritan. It was part of Christ's humiliation that he was born of the Jewish nation, which was <hi type="italic">now</hi> not only in an <hi type="italic">ill state,</hi> subject to the Romans, but in an <hi type="italic">ill name</hi> among the nations. With what disdain did Pilate ask, <hi type="italic">Am I a Jew?</hi> Thus he <hi type="italic">made himself</hi> not only <hi type="italic">of no reputation,</hi> but of <hi type="italic">ill reputation;</hi> but herein he has set us an example of swimming against the stream of common corruptions. We must, like our master, put on <hi type="italic">goodness</hi> and <hi type="italic">kindness,</hi> though it should be ever so much the genius of our country, or the humour of our party, to be morose and ill-natured. This woman expected that Christ should be as other Jews were; but it is unjust to charge upon every individual person even the common faults of the community: no rule but has some exceptions. 2. She wonders that he should <hi type="italic">expect to receive</hi> this kindness from her that was a Samaritan: "You Jews could deny it to one of our nation, and why should we grant it to one of yours?" Thus quarrels are propagated endlessly by revenge and retaliation. <div eID="gen26876" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26877" type="x-p"/> [3.] Christ takes this occasion to instruct her in divine things: <hi type="italic">If thou knewest the gift of God, thou wouldst have asked,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.4.10">v. 10</reference>. Observe, <div eID="gen26877" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26878" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> He waives her objection of the feud between the Jews and Samaritans, and takes no notice of it. Some differences are best <hi type="italic">healed</hi> by being <hi type="italic">slighted,</hi> and by avoiding all occasions of <hi type="italic">entering into dispute</hi> about them. Christ will convert this woman, not by showing her that the Samaritan worship was <hi type="italic">schismatical</hi> (though really it was so), but by showing her her own ignorance and immoralities, and her need of a Saviour. <div eID="gen26878" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26879" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> He fills her with an apprehension that she had now an opportunity (a fairer opportunity than she was aware of) of gaining that which would be of unspeakable advantage to her. She had not the helps that the Jews had to discern the signs of the times, and therefore Christ tells her expressly that she had now a season of grace; this was <hi type="italic">the day of her visitation.</hi> <div eID="gen26879" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26880" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">a.</hi> He hints to her what she <hi type="italic">should know,</hi> but was ignorant of: <hi type="italic">If thou knewest the gift of God,</hi> that is, as the next words explain it, <hi type="italic">who it is that saith, Give me to drink.</hi> If thou knewest <hi type="italic">who I am.</hi> She saw him to be a Jew, a poor weary traveller; but he would have her know something more concerning him that did yet appear. Note, (<hi type="italic">a.</hi>) Jesus Christ is the <hi type="italic">gift of God,</hi> the richest token of God's love to us, and the richest treasure of all good for us; <hi type="italic">a gift,</hi> not a debt which we could demand from God; not a <hi type="italic">loan,</hi> which he will demand from us again, but a gift, a free gift, <reference osisRef="John.3.16">ch. iii. 16</reference>. (<hi type="italic">b.</hi>) It is an unspeakable privilege to have this gift of God proposed and offered to us; to have an opportunity of embracing it: "He who is the gift of God is now set before thee, and addresses himself to <hi type="italic">thee;</hi> it is he that saith, <hi type="italic">Give me to drink;</hi> this gift comes a begging to thee." (<hi type="italic">c.</hi>) Though Christ is set before us, and sues to us in and by his gospel, yet there are multitudes that <hi type="italic">know him not.</hi> They know not who it is that speaks to them in the gospel, that saith, <hi type="italic">Give me to drink;</hi> they perceive not that it is the Lord that calls them. <div eID="gen26880" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26881" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">b.</hi> He hopes concerning her, what she would have done if she had known him; to be sure she would not have given him such a rude and uncivil answer; nay, she would have been so far from affronting him that she would have made her addresses to him: <hi type="italic">Thou wouldest have asked.</hi> Note, (<hi type="italic">a.</hi>) Those that would have any benefit by Christ must ask for it, must be earnest in prayer to God for it. (<hi type="italic">b.</hi>) Those that have a right knowledge of Christ will seek to him, and if we do not seek unto him it is a sign that we do not know him, <reference osisRef="Ps.9.10">Ps. ix. 10</reference>. (<hi type="italic">c.</hi>) Christ knows what they that want the means of knowledge would have done if they had had them, <reference osisRef="Matt.11.21">Matt. xi. 21</reference>. <div eID="gen26881" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26882" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">c.</hi> He assures her what he would have done for her if she had applied to him: "He <hi type="italic">would have given thee</hi> (and not have upbraided thee as thou doest me) <hi type="italic">living water.</hi>" By this living water is meant the <hi type="italic">Spirit,</hi> who is not like the water in the bottom of the well, for some of which he asked, but like <hi type="italic">living</hi> or <hi type="italic">running</hi> water, which was much more valuable. Note, (<hi type="italic">a.</hi>) The Spirit of grace is as <hi type="italic">living water;</hi> see <reference osisRef="John.7.38">ch. vii. 38</reference>. Under this similitude the blessings of the Messiah had been promised in the Old Testament, <reference osisRef="Isa.12.3">Isa. xii. 3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.35.7">xxxv. 7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.44.4">xliv. 3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.55.1">lv. 1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.14.8">Zech. xiv. 8</reference>. The graces of the Spirit, and his comforts, satisfy the thirsting soul, that knows its own nature and necessity. (<hi type="italic">b.</hi>) Jesus Christ <hi type="italic">can</hi> and <hi type="italic">will</hi> give the Holy Spirit to them that ask him; for he <hi type="italic">received</hi> that he might <hi type="italic">give.</hi> <div eID="gen26882" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26883" type="x-p"/> [4.] The woman objects against and cavils at the gracious intimation which Christ gave her (<reference osisRef="John.4.11-John.4.12">v. 11, 12</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thou hast nothing to draw with;</hi> and besides, <hi type="italic">Art thou greater than our father Jacob?</hi> What he spoke figuratively, she took literally; Nicodemus did so too. See what confused notions they have of spiritual things who are wholly taken up with the things that are sensible. Some respect she pays to this person, in calling him <hi type="italic">Sir,</hi> or <hi type="italic">Lord;</hi> but little respect to what he said, which she does but banter. <div eID="gen26883" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26884" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> She does not think him capable of furnishing her with any water, no, not this in the well that is just at hand: <hi type="italic">Thou has nothing to draw with,</hi> and <hi type="italic">the well is deep.</hi> This she said, not knowing the power of Christ, for he who <hi type="italic">causeth the vapours</hi> to ascend from the ends of the earth needs <hi type="italic">nothing to draw.</hi> But there are those who will trust Christ no further than they can see him, and will not believe his promise, unless the means of the performance of it be <hi type="italic">visible;</hi> as if he were tied to our methods, and could not draw water without our buckets. She asks scornfully, "<hi type="italic">Whence hast thou this living water?</hi> I see not whence thou canst have it." Note, The springs of that living water which Christ has for those that come to him are secret and undiscovered. The fountain of life is hid with Christ. Christ has enough for us, though we see not whence he has it. <div eID="gen26884" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26885" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> She does not think it possible that he should furnish her with any better water than this which she could come at, but he could not: <hi type="italic">Art thou greater than our father Jacob, who gave us the well?</hi> <div eID="gen26885" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26886" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">a.</hi> We will suppose the tradition true, that Jacob <hi type="italic">himself, and his children, and cattle, did drink of this well.</hi> And we may observe from it, (<hi type="italic">a.</hi>) The power and providence of God, in the continuance of the fountains of water from generation to generation, by the constant circulation of the rivers, like the blood in the body (<reference osisRef="Eccl.1.7">Eccl. i. 7</reference>), to which circulation perhaps the flux and reflux of the sea, like the pulses of the heart, contribute. (<hi type="italic">b.</hi>) The plainness of the patriarch Jacob; his drink was water, and he and his children drank of the same well with his cattle. <div eID="gen26886" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26887" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">b.</hi> Yet, allowing that to be true, she was out in several things; as, (<hi type="italic">a.</hi>) In calling Jacob <hi type="italic">father.</hi> What authority had the Samaritans to reckon themselves of the seed of Jacob? They were descended from that mixed multitude which the king of Assyria had placed in the cities of Samaria; what have they to do then with Jacob? Because they were the <hi type="italic">invaders</hi> of Israel's rights, and the unjust possessors of Israel's lands, were they therefore the <hi type="italic">inheritors</hi> of Israel's blood and honour? How absurd were those pretensions! (<hi type="italic">b.</hi>) She is out in claiming this well as Jacob's gift, whereas he did no more give it than Moses gave the <hi type="italic">manna,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.6.32">ch. vi. 32</reference>. But thus we are apt to call the <hi type="italic">messengers</hi> of God's gifts the <hi type="italic">donors</hi> of them, and to look so much at the hands they <hi type="italic">pass through</hi> as to forget the hand they <hi type="italic">come from.</hi> Jacob gave it to his sons, not to <hi type="italic">them.</hi> Yet thus the church's enemies not only <hi type="italic">usurp,</hi> but monopolize, the church's privileges. (<hi type="italic">c.</hi>) She was out in speaking of Christ as not worthy to be compared with our father Jacob. An over-fond veneration for antiquity makes God's graces, in the good people of our own day, to be slighted. <div eID="gen26887" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26888" type="x-p"/> [5.] Christ answers this cavil, and makes it out that the <hi type="italic">living water</hi> he had to give was far better than that of Jacob's well, <reference osisRef="John.4.13-John.4.14">v. 13, 14</reference>. Though she spoke perversely, Christ did not cast her off, but instructed and encouraged her. He shows her, <div eID="gen26888" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26889" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> That the water of Jacob's well yielded but a <hi type="italic">transient</hi> satisfaction and supply: "<hi type="italic">Whoso drinketh of this water shall thirst again.</hi> It is no better than other water; it will quench the present thirst, but the thirst will return, and in a few hours a man will have as much <hi type="italic">need,</hi> and as much <hi type="italic">desire,</hi> of water as ever he had." This intimates, 1. The <hi type="italic">infirmities</hi> of our bodies in this present state; they are still <hi type="italic">necessitous,</hi> and ever <hi type="italic">craving.</hi> Life is a <hi type="italic">fire,</hi> a <hi type="italic">lamp,</hi> which will soon go out, without continual supplies of fuel and oil. The natural heat preys upon itself. 2. The <hi type="italic">imperfections</hi> of all our comforts in this world; they are not lasting, nor our satisfaction in them remaining. Whatever waters of comfort we drink of, we shall <hi type="italic">thirst again.</hi> Yesterday's meat and drink will not do to-day's work. <div eID="gen26889" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26890" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> That the living waters he would give should yield a lasting satisfaction and bliss, <reference osisRef="John.4.14">v. 14</reference>. Christ's gifts appear most valuable when they come to be compared with the things of this world; for there will appear no comparison between them. Whoever partakes of the Spirit of grace, and the comforts of the everlasting gospel, <div eID="gen26890" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26891" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">a.</hi> He shall <hi type="italic">never thirst,</hi> he shall never want that which will abundantly satisfy his soul's desires; they are <hi type="italic">longing,</hi> but not <hi type="italic">languishing.</hi> A <hi type="italic">desiring</hi> thirst he has, nothing more <hi type="italic">than</hi> God, still more and more <hi type="italic">of</hi> God; but not a <hi type="italic">despairing</hi> thirst. <div eID="gen26891" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26892" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">b.</hi> Therefore he shall never thirst, because this water that Christ gives <hi type="italic">shall be in him a well of water. He</hi> can never be reduced to extremity that has in himself a <hi type="italic">fountain</hi> of supply and satisfaction. (<hi type="italic">a.</hi>) <hi type="italic">Ever ready,</hi> for it shall be <hi type="italic">in him.</hi> The principle of grace planted <hi type="italic">in him</hi> is the spring of his comfort; see <reference osisRef="John.7.38">ch. vii. 38</reference>. A good man is <hi type="italic">satisfied from himself,</hi> for Christ <hi type="italic">dwells in his heart.</hi> The anointing abides in him; he needs not sneak to the world for comfort; the <hi type="italic">work</hi> and the <hi type="italic">witness</hi> of the Spirit in the heart furnish him with a firm foundation of hope and an overflowing fountain of joy. (<hi type="italic">b.</hi>) <hi type="italic">Never failing,</hi> for it shall be in him a <hi type="italic">well of water.</hi> He that has at hand only a bucket of water needs not thirst as long as this lasts, but it will soon be <hi type="italic">exhausted;</hi> but believers have in them a <hi type="italic">well of water,</hi> overflowing, ever flowing. The <hi type="italic">principles</hi> and <hi type="italic">affections</hi> which Christ's holy religion <hi type="italic">forms</hi> in the souls of those that are brought under the power of it are this <hi type="italic">well of water.</hi> [<hi type="italic">a.</hi>] It is <hi type="italic">springing up,</hi> ever in motion, which bespeaks the actings of grace strong and vigorous. If good truths <hi type="italic">stagnate</hi> in our souls, like standing water, they do not answer the end of our receiving them. If there be a good treasure in the heart, we must thence bring forth good things. [<hi type="italic">b.</hi>] It is springing up <hi type="italic">unto everlasting life;</hi> which intimates, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> The <hi type="italic">aims</hi> of gracious actings. A sanctified soul has its eye upon heaven, means this, designs this, does all for this, will take up with nothing short of this. Spiritual life springs up towards its own perfection in eternal life. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> The <hi type="italic">constancy</hi> of those actings; it will continue springing up till it come to perfection. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> The crown of them, eternal life at last. The living water rises <hi type="italic">from</hi> heaven, and therefore rises <hi type="italic">towards</hi> heaven; see <reference osisRef="Eccl.1.7">Eccl. i. 7</reference>. And now is not this water better than that of Jacob's well? <div eID="gen26892" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26893" type="x-p"/> [6.] The woman (whether in jest or earnest is hard to say) begs of him to give her some of this water (<reference osisRef="John.4.15">v. 15</reference>): <hi type="italic">Give me this water, that I thirst not. First,</hi> Some think that she speaks <hi type="italic">tauntingly,</hi> and ridicules what Christ had said as mere stuff; and, in derision of it, not <hi type="italic">desires,</hi> but <hi type="italic">challenges</hi> him to give her some of this water: "A rare invention; it will save me a great deal of <hi type="italic">pains</hi> if I never <hi type="italic">come hither to draw.</hi>" But, <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Others think that it was a <hi type="italic">well-meant</hi> but weak and ignorant desire. She apprehended that he meant something very good and useful, and therefore saith <hi type="italic">Amen,</hi> at a venture. <hi type="italic">Whatever it be,</hi> let me have it; <hi type="italic">who will show me any good? Ease,</hi> or saving of labour, is a valuable good to poor labouring people. Note, 1. Even those that are weak and ignorant may yet have some faint and fluctuating desires towards Christ and his gifts, and some good wishes of grace and glory. 2. Carnal hearts, in their best wishes, look no higher than carnal ends. "Give it to me," saith she, "not that I may have everlasting life" (which Christ proposed), "but that I <hi type="italic">come not hither to draw.</hi>" <div eID="gen26893" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26894" type="x-p"/> 2. The next subject of discourse with this woman in <hi type="italic">concerning her husband,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.4.16-John.4.18">v. 16-18</reference>. It was not to let fall the discourse of the water of life that Christ started this, as many who will bring in any <hi type="italic">impertinence</hi> in conversation that they may drop a serious subject; but it was with a gracious design that Christ mentioned it. What he had said concerning his grace and eternal life he found had made little impression upon her, because she had not been convinced of sin: therefore, waiving the discourse about the living water, he sets himself to awaken her conscience, to open the wound of guilt, and then she would more easily apprehend the remedy by grace. And this is the method of dealing with souls; they must first be made <hi type="italic">weary</hi> and <hi type="italic">heavy-laden</hi> under the burden of sin, and then brought to Christ for rest; first pricked to the heart, and then healed. This is the course of spiritual physic; and if we proceed not in this order we begin at the wrong end. <div eID="gen26894" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26895" type="x-p"/> Observe, (1.) How discreetly and decently Christ introduces this discourse (<reference osisRef="John.4.16">v. 16</reference>): <hi type="italic">Go, call thy husband, and come hither.</hi> Now, [1.] The order Christ gave her had a <hi type="italic">very good colour: "Call thy husband,</hi> that he may teach thee, and help thee to understand these things, which thou art so ignorant of" The wives that will learn must <hi type="italic">ask their husbands</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Cor.14.35">1 Cor. xiv. 35</reference>), who must dwell with them <hi type="italic">as men of knowledge,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Pet.3.7">1 Pet. iii. 7</reference>. "<hi type="italic">Call thy husband,</hi> that he may learn with thee; that then you may be <hi type="italic">heirs together of the grace of life. Call thy husband,</hi> that he may be witness to what passes between us." Christ would thus teach us to <hi type="italic">provide things honest in the sight of all men,</hi> and to study that which is of good report. [2.] As it had a good colour, so it had a <hi type="italic">good design;</hi> for hence he would take occasion to call her sin to remembrance. There is need of art and prudence in giving reproofs; to fetch a compass, as the woman of Tekoa, <reference osisRef="2Sam.14.20">2 Sam. xiv. 20</reference>. <div eID="gen26895" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26896" type="x-p"/> (2.) How industriously the woman seeks to evade the conviction, and yet insensibly convicts herself, and, ere she is aware, owns her fault; she said, <hi type="italic">I have no husband.</hi> Her saying this intimated no more than that she did not care to have her husband spoken of, nor that matter mentioned any more. She would not have her husband come thither, lest, in further discourse, the truth of the matter should come out, to her shame; and therefore, "Pray go on to talk of something else, <hi type="italic">I have no husband;</hi>" she would be thought a <hi type="italic">maid</hi> or a <hi type="italic">widow,</hi> whereas, though she had no husband, she was neither. The carnal mind is very ingenious to <hi type="italic">shift off</hi> convictions, and to keep them from fastening, careful to <hi type="italic">cover the sin.</hi> <div eID="gen26896" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26897" type="x-p"/> (3.) How closely our Lord Jesus brings home the conviction to her conscience. It is probable that he said more than is here recorded, for she thought that he told her all that ever she did (<reference osisRef="John.4.29">v. 29</reference>), but that which is here recorded is concerning her husbands. Here is, [1.] A <hi type="italic">surprising narrative</hi> of her <hi type="italic">past</hi> conversation: <hi type="italic">Thou has had five husbands.</hi> Doubtless, it was not her <hi type="italic">affliction</hi> (the burying of so many husbands), but her <hi type="italic">sin,</hi> that Christ intended to upbraid her with; either she had <hi type="italic">eloped</hi> (as the law speaks), had run away from her <hi type="italic">husbands,</hi> and married others, or by her undutiful, unclean, disloyal conduct, had provoked them to <hi type="italic">divorce her,</hi> or by indirect means had, contrary to law, <hi type="italic">divorced them.</hi> Those who make light of such scandalous practices as these, as no more than <hi type="italic">nine days' wonder,</hi> and as if the guilt were over as soon as the talk is over, should remember that Christ keeps account of all. [2.] A severe reproof of her present state of life: <hi type="italic">He whom thou now hast is not thy husband.</hi> Either she was never married to him at all, or he had some other wife, or, which is most probable, her former husband or husbands were living: so that, in short, <hi type="italic">she lived in adultery.</hi> Yet observe how mildly Christ tells her of it; he doth not call her <hi type="italic">strumpet,</hi> but tells her, <hi type="italic">He with whom thou livest is not thy husband:</hi> and then leaves it to her own conscience to say the rest. Note, Reproofs are ordinarily <hi type="italic">most profitable</hi> when they are <hi type="italic">least provoking.</hi> [3.] Yet in this he puts a better construction than it would well bear upon what she said by way of shuffle and evasion: <hi type="italic">Thou has well said I have no husband;</hi> and again, <hi type="italic">In that saidst thou truly.</hi> What she intended as a <hi type="italic">denial of the fact</hi> (that she had none with whom she lived as a husband) he favourably interpreted, or at least turned upon her, as a <hi type="italic">confession of the fault.</hi> Note, Those who would win souls should <hi type="italic">make the best</hi> of them, whereby they may hope to <hi type="italic">work</hi> upon their <hi type="italic">good-nature;</hi> for, if they <hi type="italic">make the worst</hi> of them, they certainly <hi type="italic">exasperate</hi> their <hi type="italic">ill-nature.</hi> <div eID="gen26897" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26898" type="x-p"/> 3. The next subject of discourse with this woman is concerning <hi type="italic">the place of worship,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.4.19-John.4.24">v. 19-24</reference>. Observe, <div eID="gen26898" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26899" type="x-p"/> (1.) A case of conscience proposed to Christ by the woman, concerning the place of worship, <reference osisRef="John.4.19-John.4.20">v. 19, 20</reference>. <div eID="gen26899" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26900" type="x-p"/> [1.] The inducement she had to put this case: <hi type="italic">Sir, I perceive that thou art a prophet.</hi> She does not deny the truth of what he had charged her with, but by her silence owns the justice of the reproof; nor is she put into a passion by it, as many are when they are touched in a sore place, does not impute his censure to the general disgust the Jews had to the Samaritans, but (which is a rare thing) can bear to be told of a fault. But this is not all; she goes further: <hi type="italic">First,</hi> She speaks respectfully to him, calls him <hi type="italic">Sir.</hi> Thus should we <hi type="italic">honour</hi> those that deal faithfully with us. This was the effect of Christ's meekness in reproving her; he gave her no ill language, and then she gave him none. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> She acknowledges him to be a <hi type="italic">prophet,</hi> one that had a correspondence with Heaven. Note, The power of the word of Christ in searching the heart, and convincing the conscience of secret sins, is a great proof of its divine authority, <reference osisRef="1Cor.14.24-1Cor.14.25">1 Cor. xiv. 24, 25</reference>. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> She desires some further instruction from him. Many that are not <hi type="italic">angry</hi> at their reprovers, nor fly in their faces, yet are <hi type="italic">afraid</hi> of them and keep out of their way; but this woman was willing to have some more discourse with him that told her of her faults. <div eID="gen26900" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26901" type="x-p"/> [2.] The case itself that she propounded concerning the <hi type="italic">place of religious worship in public.</hi> Some think that she started this to shift off further discourse concerning her sin. Controversies in religion often prove great prejudices to serious godliness; but, it should seem, she proposed it with a good design; she knew she must worship God, and desired to do it aright; and therefore, meeting with a prophet, begs his direction. Note, It is our wisdom to improve all opportunities of getting knowledge in the things of God. When we are in company with those that are <hi type="italic">fit to teach,</hi> let us be <hi type="italic">forward to learn,</hi> and have a <hi type="italic">good question</hi> ready to put to those who are able to give a <hi type="italic">good answer.</hi> It was agreed between the Jews and the Samaritans that God is to be worshipped (even those who were such fools as to worship <hi type="italic">false</hi> gods were not such brutes as to worship none), and that religious worship is an affair of great importance: men would not <hi type="italic">contend</hi> about it if they were not <hi type="italic">concerned</hi> about it. But the matter in variance was <hi type="italic">where</hi> they should worship God. Observe how she states the case:— <div eID="gen26901" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26902" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> As for the Samaritans: <hi type="italic">Our fathers worshipped in this mountain,</hi> near to this city and this well; there the Samaritan temple was built by Sanballat, in favour of which she insinuates, 1. That whatever the temple was the place was holy; it was mount <hi type="italic">Gerizim,</hi> the mount in which the blessings were pronounced; and some think the same on which Abraham built his altar (<reference osisRef="Gen.12.6-Gen.12.7">Gen. xii. 6, 7</reference>), and Jacob his, <reference osisRef="Gen.33.18-Gen.33.20">Gen. xxxiii. 18-20</reference>. 2. That it might plead prescription: <hi type="italic">Our fathers</hi> worshipped here. She thinks they have antiquity, tradition, and succession, on their side. A <hi type="italic">vain conversation</hi> often supports itself with this, that it was <hi type="italic">received by tradition from our fathers.</hi> But she had little reason to boast of <hi type="italic">their fathers;</hi> for, when Antiochus persecuted the Jews, the Samaritans, for fear of sharing with them in their sufferings, not only renounced all relation to the Jews, but surrendered their temple to Antiochus, with a request that it might be dedicated to Jupiter Olympius, and called by his name. Joseph. <hi type="italic">Antiq.</hi> 12. 257-264. <div eID="gen26902" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26903" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> As to the Jews: <hi type="italic">You say</hi> that <hi type="italic">in Jerusalem is the place where men ought to worship.</hi> The Samaritans governed themselves by the five books of Moses, and (some think) received <hi type="italic">only them</hi> as canonical. Now, though they found frequent mention there of the place God would choose, yet they did not find it named there; and they saw the temple at Jerusalem stripped of many of its ancient glories, and therefore thought themselves at liberty to set up another place, altar against altar. <div eID="gen26903" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26904" type="x-p"/> (2.) Christ's answer to this case of conscience, <reference osisRef="John.4.21">v. 21</reference>, &c. Those that apply themselves to Christ for instruction shall find him <hi type="italic">meek, to teach the meek his way.</hi> Now here, <div eID="gen26904" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26905" type="x-p"/> [1.] He puts <hi type="italic">a slight</hi> upon the question, as she had proposed it, concerning the place of worship (<reference osisRef="John.4.21">v. 21</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Woman, believe me</hi> as a prophet, and mark what I say. Thou art expecting the <hi type="italic">hour to come</hi> when either by some divine revelation, or some signal providence, this matter shall be decided in favour either of Jerusalem or of Mount Gerizim; but I tell thee the hour is at hand when it shall be no more a question; that which thou has been taught to lay so much weight on shall be set aside as a thing <hi type="italic">indifferent.</hi>" Note, It should cool us in our contests to think that those things which now fill us, and which we make such a noise about, shall shortly <hi type="italic">vanish,</hi> and be <hi type="italic">no more:</hi> the very things we are striving about are passing away: <hi type="italic">The hour comes when you shall neither in this mountain nor yet at Jerusalem worship the Father. First,</hi> The object of worship is supposed to continue still the same—<hi type="italic">God,</hi> as a Father; under this notion the very heathen worshipped God, the Jews did so, and probably the Samaritans. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> But a period shall be put to all niceness and all differences about the place of worship. The approaching dissolution of the Jewish economy, and the erecting of the evangelical state, shall set this matter <hi type="italic">at large,</hi> and lay all <hi type="italic">in common,</hi> so that it shall be a thing perfectly indifferent whether in either of these places or any other men worship God, for they shall not be tied to any place; neither <hi type="italic">here</hi> nor <hi type="italic">there,</hi> but <hi type="italic">both,</hi> and <hi type="italic">any where,</hi> and <hi type="italic">every where.</hi> Note, The worship of God is not now, under the gospel, appropriated to any place, as it was under the law, but it is God's will that men pray every where. <reference osisRef="1Tim.2.8">1 Tim. ii. 8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mal.1.11">Mal. i. 11</reference>. Our reason teaches us to consult <hi type="italic">decency</hi> and <hi type="italic">convenience</hi> in the places of our worship: but our religion gives no preference to one place above another, in respect to holiness and acceptableness to God. Those who prefer any worship merely for the sake of the house or building in which it is performed (though it were as magnificent and as <hi type="italic">solemnly</hi> consecrated as ever Solomon's temple was) forget that the <hi type="italic">hour is come</hi> when there shall be no difference put in God's account: no, not between Jerusalem, which <hi type="italic">had been</hi> so famous for sanctity, and the mountain of Samaria, which <hi type="italic">had been</hi> so infamous for impiety. <div eID="gen26905" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26906" type="x-p"/> [2.] He <hi type="italic">lays a stress</hi> upon other things, in the matter of religious worship. When he made so light of the place of worship he did not intend to lessen our concern about the thing itself, of which therefore he takes occasion to discourse more fully. <div eID="gen26906" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26907" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> As to the present state of the controversy, he <hi type="italic">determines</hi> against the Samaritan worship, and in favour of the Jews, <reference osisRef="John.4.22">v. 22</reference>. He tells here, 1. That the Samaritans were certainly <hi type="italic">in the wrong;</hi> not merely because they worshipped in this mountain, though, while Jerusalem's choice was in force, that was sinful, but because they were out in the object of their worship. If the worship itself had been as it should have been, its separation from Jerusalem might have been connived at, as the <hi type="italic">high places</hi> were in the best reigns: <hi type="italic">But you worship you know not what,</hi> or <hi type="italic">that which you do not know.</hi> They worshipped the God of Israel, the true God (<reference osisRef="Ezra.4.2">Ezra iv. 2</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.17.32">2 Kings xvii. 32</reference>); but they were sunk into gross ignorance; they worshipped him as the <hi type="italic">God of that land</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.17.27">2 Kings xvii. 27</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.17.33">33</reference>), as a local deity, like the gods of the nations, whereas God must be served <hi type="italic">as God,</hi> as the universal cause and Lord. Note, Ignorance is so far from being the <hi type="italic">mother</hi> of devotion that it is the <hi type="italic">murderer</hi> of it. Those that worship God <hi type="italic">ignorantly</hi> offer the <hi type="italic">blind for sacrifice,</hi> and it is the <hi type="italic">sacrifice of fools.</hi> 2. That the Jews were certainly <hi type="italic">in the right.</hi> For, (1.) "<hi type="italic">We know what we worship.</hi> We go upon sure grounds in our worship, for our people are catechised and trained up in the knowledge of God, as he has revealed himself in the scripture." Note, Those who by the scriptures have obtained some knowledge of God (a <hi type="italic">certain</hi> though not a <hi type="italic">perfect</hi> knowledge) may worship him <hi type="italic">comfortably</hi> to themselves, and <hi type="italic">acceptably</hi> to him, for they <hi type="italic">know what they worship.</hi> Christ elsewhere condemns the corruptions of the Jews' worship (<reference osisRef="Matt.15.9">Matt. xv. 9</reference>), and yet here defends the worship itself; the worship may be <hi type="italic">true</hi> where yet it is not <hi type="italic">pure</hi> and <hi type="italic">entire.</hi> Observe, Our Lord Jesus was pleased to reckon himself among the <hi type="italic">worshippers</hi> of God: <hi type="italic">We worship. Though he was a Son</hi> (and then are the children free), <hi type="italic">yet learned he this obedience,</hi> in the days of his humiliation. Let not the greatest of men think the worship of God below them, when the Son of God himself did not. (2.) <hi type="italic">Salvation is of the Jews;</hi> and therefore they know what they worship, and what grounds they go upon in their worship. Not that all the Jews were saved, nor that it was not possible but that many of the Gentiles and Samaritans might be saved, for in <hi type="italic">every nation</hi> he that fears God and works righteousness is <hi type="italic">accepted of him;</hi> but, [1.] The author of eternal salvation comes of the Jews, appears among them (<reference osisRef="Rom.9.5">Rom. ix. 5</reference>), and is sent first to <hi type="italic">bless</hi> them. [2.] The means of eternal salvation are afforded to them. The <hi type="italic">word of salvation</hi> (<reference osisRef="Acts.13.26">Acts xiii. 26</reference>) was <hi type="italic">of the Jews.</hi> It was delivered to them, and other nations derived it through them. This was a sure guide to them in their devotions, and they followed it, and therefore knew what they worshipped. To them were committed the <hi type="italic">oracles of God</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rom.3.2">Rom. iii. 2</reference>), and the <hi type="italic">service of God,</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rom.9.4">Rom. ix. 4</reference>). The Jews therefore being thus privileged and advanced, it was presumption for the Samaritans to vie with them. <div eID="gen26907" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26908" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> He describes the evangelical worship which alone God would accept and be well pleased with. Having shown that the place is <hi type="italic">indifferent,</hi> he comes to show what is <hi type="italic">necessary</hi> and <hi type="italic">essential</hi>—that we worship God <hi type="italic">in spirit and in truth,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.4.23-John.4.24">v. 23, 24</reference>. The stress is not to be laid upon the <hi type="italic">place</hi> where we worship God, but upon the state of <hi type="italic">mind</hi> in which we worship him. Note, The most effectual way to take up differences in the minor matters of religion is to be more zealous in the greater. Those who daily make it the matter of their care to worship <hi type="italic">in the spirit,</hi> one would think, should not make it the matter of their strife whether he should be worshipped here or there. Christ had justly preferred the Jewish worship before the Samaritan, yet here he intimates the imperfection of that. The worship was <hi type="italic">ceremonial,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.9.1">Heb. ix. 1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.9.10">10</reference>. The worshippers were generally <hi type="italic">carnal,</hi> and strangers to the <hi type="italic">inward part</hi> of divine worship. Note, It is possible that we may be better than our neighbours, and yet not so good as we should be. It concerns us to be right, not only in the <hi type="italic">object</hi> of our worship, but in the <hi type="italic">manner</hi> of it; and it is this which Christ here instructs us in. Observe, <div eID="gen26908" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26909" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">a.</hi> The great and glorious revolution which should introduce this change: <hi type="italic">The hour cometh, and now is</hi>—the fixed stated time, concerning which it was of old determined when it should come, and how long it should last. The time of its <hi type="italic">appearance</hi> if <hi type="italic">fixed</hi> to an hour, so punctual and exact are the divine counsels; the time of its <hi type="italic">continuance</hi> is <hi type="italic">limited</hi> to an hour, so close and pressing is the opportunity of divine grace, <reference osisRef="2Cor.6.2">2 Cor. vi. 2</reference>. This hour <hi type="italic">cometh,</hi> it is coming in its full strength, lustre, and perfection, it <hi type="italic">now is</hi> in the embryo and infancy. The <hi type="italic">perfect day is coming,</hi> and now it <hi type="italic">dawns.</hi> <div eID="gen26909" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26910" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">b.</hi> The blessed change itself. In gospel times the <hi type="italic">true worshippers shall worship the Father in spirit and in truth.</hi> As creatures, we worship the Father of <hi type="italic">all:</hi> as Christians, we worship <hi type="italic">the Father of our Lord Jesus.</hi> Now the change shall be, (<hi type="italic">a.</hi>) In the <hi type="italic">nature</hi> of the worship. Christians shall worship God, not in the ceremonial observances of the Mosaic institution, but in <hi type="italic">spiritual</hi> ordinances, consisting less in <hi type="italic">bodily exercise,</hi> and animated and invigorated more with divine power and energy. The way of worship which Christ has instituted is rational and intellectual, and refined from those external rites and ceremonies with which the Old-Testament worship was both clouded and clogged. This is called true worship, in opposition to that which was typical. The legal services were <hi type="italic">figures of the true,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.9.3">Heb. ix. 3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.9.24">24</reference>. Those that revolted from Christianity to Judaism are said to <hi type="italic">begin in the spirit, and end in the flesh,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gal.3.3">Gal. iii. 3</reference>. Such was the difference between Old-Testament and New-Testament institutions. (<hi type="italic">b.</hi>) In the <hi type="italic">temper</hi> and <hi type="italic">disposition</hi> of the worshippers; and so the true worshippers are good Christians, distinguished from hypocrites; all <hi type="italic">should,</hi> and they will, worship God <hi type="italic">in spirit and in truth.</hi> It is spoken of (<reference osisRef="John.4.23">v. 23</reference>) as their character, and (<reference osisRef="John.4.24">v. 24</reference>) as their duty. Note, It is required of all that worship God that they worship him <hi type="italic">in spirit and in truth.</hi> We must worship God, [<hi type="italic">a.</hi>] <hi type="italic">In spirit,</hi> <reference osisRef="Phil.3.3">Phil. iii. 3</reference>. We must depend upon <hi type="italic">God's Spirit</hi> for strength and assistance, laying our souls under his influences and operations; we must devote <hi type="italic">our own spirits</hi> to, and employ them in, the service of God (<reference osisRef="Rom.1.9">Rom. i. 9</reference>), must worship him with fixedness of thought and a flame of affection, with <hi type="italic">all that is within us.</hi> Spirit is sometimes put for the new nature, in opposition to the <hi type="italic">flesh,</hi> which is the corrupt nature; and so to worship God <hi type="italic">with our spirits</hi> is to worship him <hi type="italic">with our graces,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.12.28">Heb. xii. 28</reference>. [<hi type="italic">b.</hi>] <hi type="italic">In truth,</hi> that is, in <hi type="italic">sincerity.</hi> God requires not only the <hi type="italic">inward part</hi> in our worship, but <hi type="italic">truth in the inward part,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.51.6">Ps. li. 6</reference>. We must mind the power more than the form, must aim at God's glory, and not to be <hi type="italic">seen of men;</hi> draw near with a <hi type="italic">true heart,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.10.22">Heb. x. 22</reference>. <div eID="gen26910" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26911" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> He intimates the reasons why God must be thus worshipped. <div eID="gen26911" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26912" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">a.</hi> Because in gospel times they, and they only, are accounted the <hi type="italic">true</hi> worshippers. The gospel erects a spiritual way of worship, so that the professors of the gospel are not true in their profession, do not live up to gospel light and laws, if they do not worship God <hi type="italic">in spirit and in truth.</hi> <div eID="gen26912" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26913" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">b.</hi> Because <hi type="italic">the Father seeketh such worshippers of him.</hi> This intimates, (<hi type="italic">a.</hi>) That such worshippers are very rare, and seldom met with, <reference osisRef="Jer.30.21">Jer. xxx. 21</reference>. The gate of spiritual worshipping is strait. (<hi type="italic">b.</hi>) That such worship is necessary, and what the God of heaven insists upon. When God comes to <hi type="italic">enquire</hi> for worshippers, the question will not be, "Who worshipped at Jerusalem?" but, "Who worshipped in spirit?" That will be the touchstone. (<hi type="italic">c.</hi>) That God is greatly well pleased with and graciously accepts such worship and such worshippers. <hi type="italic">I have desired it,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.132.13-Ps.132.14">Ps. cxxxii. 13, 14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Song.2.14">Cant. ii. 14</reference>. (<hi type="italic">d.</hi>) That there has been, and will be to the end, a remnant of such worshippers; his <hi type="italic">seeking</hi> such worshippers implies his <hi type="italic">making</hi> them such. God is in all ages gathering in to himself a generation of spiritual worshippers. <div eID="gen26913" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26914" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">c.</hi> Because <hi type="italic">God is a spirit.</hi> Christ came to <hi type="italic">declare God</hi> to us (<reference osisRef="John.1.18">ch. i. 18</reference>), and this he has declared concerning him; he declared it to this poor Samaritan woman, for the meanest are concerned to know God; and with this design, to rectify her mistakes concerning religious worship, to which nothing would contribute more than the right knowledge of God.
